newsitem.title: UK: Soft tone in EU grains amid frustration on exports.
newsitem.headline: Soft tone in EU grains amid frustration on exports.

text.p: Frustration that European Union export policy is not aggressive enough to deal with its grains surplus helped to maintain a weak tone in domestic markets.
Good consumer coverage has meant a shortage of major buyers, traders said.
In the UK market the same worries exist as on the Continent, traders said, but sterling's volatility against other EU currencies has become the main driving, and destabilising, element in the market.
"It's all over the place," a UK domestic market trader said.
After a slow November, the UK was left with too much grain still to be sold, he said.
"In theoretical terms the market should be going down, but with sterling uncertain, people are reluctant to sell at lower prices," another UK trader said.

French wheat prices were steady to slightly easier on the week amid slow demand for spot grain, dealers said, adding that buyers are well covered until mid-December. But demand could pick up later this month ahead of Christmas.
The underlying price trend remained bearish on poor export prospects for EU wheat amid fierce competition from other exporters, French traders said.
News Pakistan bought 225,000 tonnes of Australian wheat bypassing U.S. wheat, confirmed U.S. prices were now out of range with world markets, traders added.

The sale was bound to increase pressure on the EU to stop pricing its wheat against U.S. wheat and grant higher wheat export refunds to start competing with cheaper supplies from Australia and Argentina.
EU grain exporters fear that unless the EU starts competing with Argentina and Australia it could lose some traditional markets in north Africa or eastern Europe.

In a move aimed at providing relief to hard pressed African customers the EU has cleared bids by EU firms to export 142,000 tonnes of wheat under short-term licences carrying a 28 Ecus per tonne refund.

The refund represents a jump of 10 Ecus on the refund granted at the November 28 tender for other non-EU destinations. French maize prices were steady on the week. Rain is disrupting the last stages of the harvest. But the damage to the crop should be marginal, local grain analysts have said. Ample maize supplies in Italy and Spain may however limit export prospects for French maize.
Spanish trading was very quiet with low demand pressurising prices downwards, dealers said.
More maize has gradually come on to the market but around 40 percent in the main northern regions where it is grown has yet to be harvested, they estimated.
Some barley and durum wheat has started to be sown in the south of Spain, but as yet this is a limited amount, they added.

In Italy the market was also quiet with most end-users well covered and transport of imports hampered by the French truckers' strike. Its effects were not severe enough to be worrying to a generally well supplied industry, traders said.
Durum wheat prices firmed with buyers making sure they were covered ahead of Christmas, but activity was scattered.
Sales of common wheat and maize in Italy were confined to routine trading with prices largely unchanged and recent cooler weather in northern Italy not having much impact.
German wheat sales remain sluggish as domestic and overseas buyers held back, brokers said on Wednesday.
Southern Europe was seen buying normal quality from France and Britain, rather than from Germany, German traders said.
Domestic German feed wheat buyers were covering much of their winter demand from Britain and Denmark.
